question: A manager has broken a customer-refund policy rewrite into five stages and wants one point at which she personally reviews the work. Where should that review sit?
options: A) After the stage that settles which refund cases are covered, because every later stage is written to that decision.
B) After the first stage, since reviewing early gives her the longest possible time to act on anything she finds.
C) At whichever stage happens to fall in the middle, which keeps the amount of unreviewed work on each side even.
D) At the very end, once all five stages are complete, so that she reviews the finished policy as customers will read it.
correct_answers: A) After the stage that settles which refund cases are covered, because every later stage is written to that decision.
explanations: Correct. A checkpoint is worth most immediately after the decision that constrains everything downstream. If the covered cases are wrong, the wording, the examples and the exceptions are all wrong too, and catching that later means rewriting all of them.
Reviewing the first stage is cheap but often premature, since the first stage may be preparatory and not yet contain the decision that matters.
Splitting by position balances the volume of unreviewed work but ignores which stage actually carries the consequential decision.
A final review catches errors at the point where correcting them means redoing the stages that followed the mistake.
